newsitem.title: RUSSIA: New crew blasts off to troubled space station.
newsitem.headline: New crew blasts off to troubled space station.

text.p: Two Russian cosmonauts blasted off without a hitch for the Mir space station on Tuesday on their way to tackle a host of problems, including a broken oxygen system, that the current Mir crew has been unable to fix.

Mission Control outside Moscow broadcast live video of Commander Anatoly Solovyov and flight engineer Pavel Vinogradov, dressed in spacesuits and strapped to their seats, as they were launched into orbit.
Solovyov waved goodbye to the camera as the slender Proton rocket lifted off from the Baikonur cosmodrome in Kazakhstan at 1536 GMT in a blaze of yellow light against the darkening evening sky.

"The launch went normally and 526 seconds after lift-off it became clear that the astronauts were in weightlessness when a talisman they had with them for good luck started floating," cosmonaut Viktor Afanasiyev told reporters.
The Baikonur launch attracted an usually high-ranking Russian delegation, including Defence Minister Igor Sergeyev and Yuri Baturin, secretary of President Boris Yeltsin's Defence Council.
On board Mir, the current crew were using canisters to supplement their oxygen as they were still unable to get the Elektron oxygen generating system to start, space officials said.
"This has happened a thousand times before, so it's not worth making a fuss about," deputy flight director Viktor Blagov told Reuters at Mission Control.
"Yes, we are concerned, yes, we are worried, but we have immense experience...in dealing with this."
The oxygen system failed to start last week and several days of work have not resolved the problem, which NASA believes is caused by air bubbles.

Mir's back-up oxygen system is also out of action because it is located in the Kvant-2 module, which the crew powered down to save energy after Mir collided with its resupply ship on June 25, causing a major loss of power.
Solovyov, 49, a four-time veteran of the Mir space station, has spent a total of 456 days in space. Vinogradov, 43, is flying for the first time but will lead the repair efforts.

The team are expected to don spacesuits on August 20 to reattach cables to the damaged Spektr module, an operation which, if successful, will restore power to much of the space station. In September they will start efforts to plug a hole in the module's exterior.

"The first task of the new crew is to re-establish the energy supply," flight director Vladimir Solovyov told reporters after the launch. "The second task is to inspect the puncture and re-establish the pressure inside the Spektr."
The repairs will be risky. Space officials say Spektr could contain dangerous floating chemicals or debris, and a puncture in a space suit could mean a swift death.

U.S. astronaut Michael Foale, the third member of the crew, will wait in the Soyuz escape vehicle during the repair. He is due to leave Mir in late September, to be replaced by David Wolf, who is currently training outside Moscow.
The two Russian crew members now on board are scheduled to return to Earth on August 14.
Responding to suggestions that Mir, whose name means 'peace' or 'world' in Russian, has outlived its usefulness, flight director Solovyov said:
"The Mir station is very important not only for the Russian space programme but also for many countries which are exploring space.
"I think the station will continue its mission in space for another five years."
